q: You update state directly like this.state.count = 1 instead of setState. The UI doesn't update. Why?
options: State is read-only in React
React only re-renders when setState or useState setter is called
You need to call forceUpdate after direct mutation
Direct mutation only works in class components
explain: React doesn't know state changed unless you use setState or a useState setter. Direct mutation bypasses React's update cycle so the UI stays stale.

q: You render a list without key props and React warns you. Why does React need keys?
options: Keys are required for CSS styling of list items
Keys help React identify which items changed, were added or removed
Keys prevent duplicate values in the list
Keys are needed for event handlers to work on list items
explain: Keys give React a stable identity for each list item during reconciliation. Without them React can't efficiently update the DOM and may reuse the wrong elements.

q: What is the difference between props and state in React?
options: Props are mutable, state is immutable
Props come from the parent, state is managed inside the component
State can be passed to children, props cannot
There is no difference — they are both ways to store data
explain: Props are passed from parent to child and are read-only. State is owned and managed by the component itself and can change over time.

q: You call useState and get [value, setValue]. What happens when you call setValue with a new value?
options: The value updates immediately in the same render
React schedules a re-render with the new value
The old value is permanently replaced in memory
setValue only works inside event handlers
explain: Calling a useState setter schedules a re-render. The new value is not available until the next render — reading the variable immediately after calling setValue still gives you the old value.

q: You want to run code after a component mounts. Which hook do you use?
options: useCallback
useMemo
useEffect with an empty dependency array
useRef
explain: useEffect with [] runs once after the initial mount. Without the array it runs after every render. With dependencies it runs when those values change.

q: A child component needs to tell the parent something happened. How do you do this in React?
options: The child modifies the parent's state directly
The parent passes a callback function as a prop, the child calls it
Use a global variable to share the event
Child components cannot communicate with parents
explain: React data flows down. To communicate upward the parent passes a callback as a prop and the child calls it with any data. This keeps data flow predictable.

q: What does React.Fragment or <> </> do?
options: Creates a new React context
Lets you return multiple elements without adding an extra DOM node
Wraps components in a performance boundary
Creates a portal to render outside the root element
explain: Fragments let you group multiple elements without adding a wrapping div to the DOM. Useful when extra DOM nodes would break layout like inside tables or flex containers.

q: You want to store a value that persists across renders but doesn't cause a re-render when it changes. What do you use?
options: useState
useEffect
useRef
useMemo
explain: useRef returns a mutable object whose .current property persists across renders. Changing it does not trigger a re-render unlike useState.

q: You pass the same props to a component but it re-renders every time the parent renders. How do you prevent this?
options: Use useCallback on the component
Wrap the component in React.memo
Move the component outside the parent file
Use shouldComponentUpdate
explain: React.memo wraps a component and skips re-rendering if props haven't changed using shallow comparison. The component only re-renders when its props actually change.

q: What is prop drilling and why is it a problem?
options: Passing too many props to one component
Passing props through multiple layers of components that don't need them
Using props instead of state for dynamic data
Drilling down into an object prop to access nested values
explain: Prop drilling is passing data through intermediate components that don't use it just to reach a deeply nested component. It makes code harder to maintain and refactor.

q: You want to share state between two sibling components. What is the React pattern for this?
options: Store the state in a global variable
Lift the state up to the nearest common parent
Use useRef in both components
Each component should have its own copy of the state
explain: Lifting state up means moving it to the closest common ancestor so it can be passed down to both siblings as props. This keeps one source of truth.

q: What is the purpose of the useContext hook?
options: To create a new context provider
To consume a value from a React context without prop drilling
To share state between unrelated components using refs
To memoize context values for performance
explain: useContext reads the current value of a context. Any component in the tree can access the context value without receiving it as a prop from every parent.

q: Your useEffect is running after every render. You only want it to run once. What is missing?
options: A return statement inside the effect
An empty dependency array as the second argument
The async keyword before the effect function
A condition inside the effect
explain: Without a dependency array useEffect runs after every render. An empty array [] tells React there are no dependencies so the effect only runs once after mount.

q: What is a controlled component in React?
options: A component wrapped in React.memo
A form element whose value is controlled by React state
A component that cannot be re-rendered by its parent
A component that manages its own internal DOM
explain: A controlled component has its value driven by React state. Every change goes through setState making React the single source of truth for the input value.

q: You want to access a DOM element directly in React. What is the correct approach?
options: Use document.getElementById inside the component
Use useRef and attach it to the element via the ref prop
Use useState to store the DOM element
Use useEffect to query the DOM after render
explain: useRef creates a ref object. Attaching it to an element via ref={myRef} gives you direct access to the DOM node at myRef.current after the component mounts.

q: What does the cleanup function returned from useEffect do?
options: It clears the component's state on unmount
It runs before the next effect execution and on unmount to clean up subscriptions or timers
It prevents the effect from running more than once
It resets props to their default values
explain: The cleanup function runs when the component unmounts and before the effect re-runs on the next render. Use it to clear timers, cancel requests, or remove event listeners.

q: You have a button click handler that updates state. Where should the handler be defined?
options: Outside the component as a global function
Inside the component so it has access to state and props
Inside the JSX as an inline string
In a separate hooks file always
explain: Handlers defined inside the component have access to state, props, and other variables in scope. Defining them outside means they lose that context.

q: What is the virtual DOM in React?
options: A copy of the DOM stored in a database
A lightweight in-memory representation of the real DOM React uses to compute updates
A browser API that React uses for fast rendering
The DOM that exists before CSS is applied
explain: The virtual DOM is a JavaScript object tree that mirrors the real DOM. React diffs the old and new virtual DOM trees to find the minimal set of real DOM changes needed.

q: You want to conditionally render a component only when a value is true. What is the cleanest approach?
options: Use a switch statement in JSX
Use the && operator: {isVisible && <Component />}
Return null from a separate function
Use CSS display none instead
explain: The && operator short-circuits — if the left side is false the right side never renders. It is the most concise way to conditionally show a component.

q: What is JSX?
options: A new programming language created by Facebook
A syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like code in JavaScript
A React function that renders components to the DOM
A JavaScript module system for React components
explain: JSX is syntactic sugar that compiles to React.createElement calls. It lets you describe UI structure in a familiar HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript files.

q: You need to update one field in a state object without losing the other fields. What is the correct way?
options: setState(newValue) — React merges automatically
setState(prev => ({ ...prev, field: newValue }))
Mutate the state object directly then call setState
Create a new useState for each field
explain: Unlike class component setState, the useState setter replaces state entirely. Spread the previous state and override only the field you want to change.

q: What is the difference between useEffect and useLayoutEffect?
options: useLayoutEffect is for animations only
useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations but before paint, useEffect runs after paint
useEffect is deprecated in React 18
They are identical — useLayoutEffect is just an alias
explain: useLayoutEffect fires synchronously after DOM updates before the browser paints. Use it when you need to read or modify the DOM before the user sees the screen to avoid flicker.

q: You want to lazy load a component only when it is needed. What do you use?
options: useEffect with a dynamic import
React.lazy with Suspense
React.memo with a loading prop
useRef to defer component creation
explain: React.lazy wraps a dynamic import and defers loading until the component is rendered. Wrap it in Suspense to show a fallback while it loads.

q: What does React.StrictMode do?
options: Prevents state mutations in production
Highlights potential problems by running certain functions twice in development
Locks component props so they cannot be changed
Enables TypeScript type checking in React
explain: StrictMode intentionally double-invokes render functions and effects in development to help you find side effects. It has no effect in production.

q: You have a component that fetches data on mount. The user navigates away before the fetch completes and you get a memory leak warning. Why?
options: fetch() does not work inside React components
The fetch resolves and tries to update state on an unmounted component
useEffect does not support async operations
The component is re-rendering too many times
explain: When the component unmounts React removes it but the fetch still resolves and calls setState. Return a cleanup function from useEffect that cancels the request or ignores the result.
